query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor fraction of a ductility-promoting element, such as titanium, into NbMoTaW (e.g., forming a NbMoTaWTi quinary alloy with roughly 5–10 at% Ti) will improve room-temperature ductility and enhance irradiation tolerance without compromising the high-temperature BCC phase stability and strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW, which retains excellent mechanical properties at high temperature (up to 1600 °C) but suffers from poor room-temperature ductility and untested experimental irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Microalloying NbMoTaW by adding approximately 5–10 atomic percent of Ti to form a quinary alloy (NbMoTaWTi).
generation.conditions: Tested over a broad temperature range (from room temperature to 1600 °C) and under irradiation conditions similar to those in previous studies (e.g., helium implantation at energies where blistering and irradiation-induced defects have been observed).
generation.structural_mediator: The incorporation of Ti is expected to slightly alter the lattice distortion of the BCC matrix, potentially creating local strain fields that act as defect sinks while preserving the overall BCC structure.
generation.mechanism: Titanium is anticipated to promote improved ductility at room temperature by facilitating dislocation motion and local atomic rearrangements, reducing brittleness. Furthermore, its presence may enhance defect recombination due to altered diffusion paths, thereby improving resistance to irradiation-induced damage such as amorphization and blistering. The altered lattice strain field can also help arrest the propagation of irradiation-induced defects while maintaining high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-modified alloy is predicted to exhibit increased plasticity and ductility at room temperature and reduced irradiation damage (lower defect densities and diminished blistering) while continuing to show high strength and phase stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The mechanical and irradiation performance metrics established for as-synthesized, equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW (noting its excellent high-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility and only computationally inferred irradiation resistance).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to hold from room temperature up to 1600 °C under irradiation conditions typical of helium implantation tests; however, extreme irradiation conditions (e.g., very high helium energies) may still induce surface or phase instabilities.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti content and its long-term effects on phase stability, diffusion kinetics, and irradiation behavior remain to be determined. There is uncertainty regarding the balance between enhancing ductility versus maintaining high-temperature strength and irradiation robustness.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with varying Ti contents (e.g., 0%, 5%, and 10% atomic Ti). Use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the retention of the single-phase BCC structure and identify any microstructural changes. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to compare ductility and yield strength, and conduct helium ion irradiation experiments, followed by nanoindentation and post-irradiation TEM to assess defect structures, irradiation hardening, and any blistering or amorphization.
measurements: Mechanical testing: room-temperature ductility (plastic strain), yield and ultimate tensile strength
Nanoindentation hardness profiles pre- and post-irradiation
Irradiation damage characterization (defect density, blistering analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and reduced irradiation damage—without a loss in high-temperature strength and BCC phase stability—compared to the baseline NbMoTaW, the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn order to find more excellent structural materials resistant to radiation damage, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been developed due to their characteristics of limited point defect diffusion such as lattice distortion and slow diffusion. Specially, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) that can adapt to a high-temperature environment are badly needed. In this study, TiZrHfNbMo0.1 RHEAs are selected for irradiation and nanoindentation experiments. We combined the mechanistic model for the depth-dependent hardness of ion-irradiated metals and the introduction of the scale factor f to modify the irradiation-hardening model in order to better describe the nanoindentation indentation process in the irradiated layer. Finally, it can be found that, with the increase in irradiation dose, a more serious lattice distortion caused by a higher defect density limits the expansion of the plastic zone.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical properties, ion irradiation, indentation size effect, plastic zone

## Abstract
AbstractMedium-entropy alloys (MEAs) have attracted considerable attention in recent decades due to their exceptional material properties and design flexibility. In this study, lightweight and non-equiatomic MEAs with low density (~5 g/cm3), high strength (yield strength: 1200 MPa), and high ductility (plastic deformation: ≧10%) were explored. We fine-tuned a previously developed Ti-rich MEA by microalloying it with small amounts of Ni (reducing the atomic radius and increasing the elastic modulus) through solid solution strengthening to achieve a series of MEAs with enhanced mechanical properties. Among the prepared MEAs, Ti65Ni1 and Ti65Ni3 exhibited optimal properties in terms of the balance between strength and ductility. Furthermore, the Ti65Ni3 MEA was subjected to thermo-mechanical treatment (TMT) followed by cold rolling 70% (CR70) and cold rolling 85% (CR85). Subsequently, the processed samples were rapidly annealed at 743 °C, 770 °C, 817 °C, and 889 °C at a heating rate of 15 °C/s.
